html:
The money cowry, a small sea shell gathered in huge numbers in the shallow lagoons of the Maldives, served as money around the Indian Ocean and beyond from at least the 10th century to the 19th.

Arab writers already knew the islands for their shells, and Ibn Battuta, who lived there in the 1340s, saw them loaded by the shipful. Cowries were small change in Bengal for centuries. Portuguese, Dutch and English ships then carried them by the ton to West Africa, where they bought enslaved people in the Atlantic slave trade.

The shells, with coconut rope, paid for the rice and cloth the islands could not make. They made the remote atolls part of the Indian Ocean trade until European coins and paper money ended their use.
sum: The money cowry, a small sea shell gathered in huge numbers in the shallow lagoons of the Maldives, served as money around the Indian Ocean and beyond from at least the 10th century to the 19th.
